nodes.label:
Energize Coil Pair 1
rotor at 0.0°
nodes.title: Energize Coil Pair 1 - rotor aligns to position 1
nodes.info: Current through the first coil pair pulls the nearest rotor teeth into line with it. The rotor is now held at a known position -- this is what makes a stepper different from a plain DC motor.

nodes.label:
Energize Coil Pair 2
advances 1.8°
nodes.title: Energize Coil Pair 2 - rotor advances 1.8 degrees
nodes.info: Switching current to the next coil pair moves the magnetic pull one tooth along, and the rotor follows by exactly 1.8 degrees. No feedback sensor is involved; the step size is a property of how the motor is built.

nodes.label:
Energize Coil Pair 3
advances 1.8°
nodes.title: Energize Coil Pair 3 - rotor advances another 1.8 degrees
nodes.info: The third pair repeats the trick. Because each step is identical, a program can count steps instead of measuring angle -- which is why steppers are used for 3D printer axes.

nodes.label:
Energize Coil Pair 4
advances 1.8°
nodes.title: Energize Coil Pair 4 - rotor advances another 1.8 degrees
nodes.info: The fourth pair completes the four-phase cycle. The rotor has now turned 5.4 degrees from where it started.

nodes.label:
Return to Coil Pair 1
cycle repeats
nodes.title: Return to Coil Pair 1 - the cycle repeats
nodes.info: The pattern loops. Each full four-step cycle advances the rotor 7.2 degrees, so fifty cycles -- two hundred steps -- make one complete rotation.

counter.label: Total rotation so far
counter.note: Click the steps in order to accumulate rotation. 200 steps -- fifty cycles -- make one full turn.
